title: Quasi-finite = locally quasi-finite + quasi-compact
statement:
Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes. Then $f$ is quasi-finite if
and only if $f$ is locally quasi-finite and quasi-compact.

proof.text: Assume first that $f$ is quasi-finite. By [pqf-def-quasifinite], it is of finite type and every point of $X$ is isolated in its fibre. The finite-type convention [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] says that a finite-type morphism is locally of finite type and quasi-compact. For any $x\in X$, choose affine neighbourhoods $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $x$ and $V=\operatorname{Spec}R$ of $f(x)$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$. The point of the fibre over $f(x)$ lying over $x$ is isolated by the hypothesis, so [lem-weil-pbc-isolated-fibre-point-quasi-finite-affine-pairs] gives that $R\to A$ is quasi-finite at the prime of $x$; hence $f$ is quasi-finite at $x$ by [pqf-def-quasifinite]. Thus $f$ is locally quasi-finite and quasi-compact. Conversely, assume that $f$ is locally quasi-finite and quasi-compact. By [lem-weil-pbc-lqf-locally-finite-type], local quasi-finiteness gives local finite type, and the convention [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] upgrades local finite type together with quasi-compactness to finite type. For each $x\in X$, quasi-finiteness at $x$ implies that the point of the fibre over $f(x)$ lying over $x$ is isolated by [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-at-point-isolated]. Hence every point is isolated in its fibre, and [pqf-def-quasifinite] gives that $f$ is quasi-finite.
